title: Perinatal Exposure to Traffic-Related Air Pollution and Atopy at 1 Year of Age in a Multi-Center Canadian Birth Cohort Study.
ehr_evidence: The CHILD study is a prospective longitudinal national birth cohort that recruited over 3,600 families between 2008 and 2012 in four Canadian cities [Vancouver, Edmonton, Winnipeg, and Toronto]
summary: A prospective multi-center birth cohort study of 2,477 children at approximately 1 year of age in four Canadian cities examining the association between perinatal traffic-related air pollution (NO2) exposure and atopy/allergic sensitization.
key_findings: TRAP exposure after birth increased the risk for development of atopy to any allergens (aOR per 10 μg/m3 NO2 = 1.16; 95% CI: 1.00, 1.41), but not during pregnancy (aOR = 1.02; 95% CI: 0.86, 1.22)
The association was stronger among children not attending daycare (aOR = 1.61; 95% CI: 1.28, 2.01) compared with daycare attendees (aOR = 1.05; 95% CI: 0.81, 1.28)
Trends to increased risk were found for food allergens (aOR = 1.17; 95% CI: 0.95, 1.47) and inhalant allergens (aOR = 1.28; 95% CI: 0.93, 1.76)
During pregnancy, effect estimates were null for sensitization to any allergens (aOR = 1.02; 95% CI: 0.86, 1.22) and food allergens (aOR = 1.00; 95% CI: 0.77, 1.61)
captured_features: City-specific land use regression NO2 exposure estimates temporally adjusted at bi-weekly intervals
Residential address history and residential mobility (time-weighted average exposure)
Atopy status defined by positive skin-prick test response to any allergen
Inhalant and food allergen sensitization clusters
Time spent away from home (time-activity patterns)
Maternal atopy, SES, furry pets, mold, nutrition, secondhand smoke
population: 2,477 children at approximately 1 year of age from four Canadian cities (Vancouver, Edmonton, Winnipeg, Toronto), recruited 2008-2012
limitations: Exposure derived from modeled LUR estimates rather than measurements, increasing error propagation
Self-reported environmental risk factors may be biased by parental health status
Bias toward higher socioeconomic status compared with the general population
Infiltration model developed for U.S. cities may not apply to Canadian homes
Missing covariates substantially reduced sample sizes for individual analyses
